title: Winnipeg's Slide Is Real, and the Chances Back It Up
dek: The Jets are 4-7-3 and winless in eight, and the numbers say the process is as bad as the results.
text:
The Jets sit 27th in the league in points with 11 from 14 games, a 4-7-3 record that looks worse by the week. They are winless in their last eight (0-6-2) and have been outscored 30-16 in that stretch. The usual comfort for a team in a slide is that the results are lying about how it has played. Here, they mostly aren't.

## How the record was built

Winnipeg has scored 34 goals and allowed 47. The chances tell the same story. Expected goals, a measure of the quality of the shots each side generates, put the Jets at 40.6 for and 49.7 against. That works out to 45% of the expected goals, 27th in the league. Their five-on-five share is also 45%, so this isn't a penalty-kill problem leaking into the totals. When the teams are even, Winnipeg is getting out-chanced.

The game-by-game arc shows how thin the margin has been. The Jets opened with an overtime loss to BOS, then won three of four, beating DET, PIT and COL by identical 3-2 scores (two of them on the road). Those wins carry a warning, though. Against DET, we estimate they deserved to win 18% of the time, a figure that comes from replaying every shot in the game thousands of times and counting how often each team comes out ahead. Against COL it was 35%. Winnipeg won both anyway.

Since that start, the results have caught up with the play, and then dropped below it. The Jets lost to ANA 5-1, beat MIN 5-2, then went 0-6-2 over the next eight, starting with the 3-4 overtime loss at CHI. The worst performances came in the most recent games. At TBL they generated 2.21 expected goals to 4.34 against (a 24% chance to win), and in the 5-2 loss at FLA on Friday it was 2.49 to 4.66 (25%). Those weren't unlucky nights. Winnipeg was beaten on the chances.

There is one real exception. At home against MTL on October 25, the Jets out-chanced the Canadiens 3.84 to 2.98, a 63% deserved-to-win figure, and lost 2-1. That was their best performance of the season by that measure and it produced nothing.

## Finishing and goaltending

Two pieces of the picture pull in different directions. Winnipeg has scored 6.6 fewer goals than its chances would predict, so shooting luck has hurt. The leaguewide average is zero, and a gap that size is partly bad finishing and partly bounces, and it tends to shrink over a longer season. Meanwhile, the goaltending has actually helped. Goals saved above expected, which compares the goals a goalie allowed to what an average goalie would have allowed on the same shots, is +2.7 for the team.

That figure hides a split. Stuart Skinner has started nine games with a .899 save percentage and +4.06 goals saved above expected. Clay Stevenson has started four, with a .870 save percentage and -1.63. Last season Skinner was at +5.96 and Stevenson at +3.1, so neither is far from his recent form in a bad way. The goaltending isn't the reason Winnipeg is losing. The Jets are giving up too many good chances for anyone to bail them out.

As reporter Mike Fink of The Hockey News put it on October 30, "The Winnipeg Jets have lost 7 games in a row," before listing the next six opponents. The Free Press's Ken Wiebe, meanwhile, posted on October 28 about the Jets "dropping a sixth consecutive game," and also linked a piece on former coach Paul Maurice discussing "the departure of Connor Hellebuyck." We can't tell you what that departure has meant in the room, but the goalie position is clearly part of what is being talked about around this team.

## Special teams

The power play ranks 16th, producing 0.67 expected goals per game. That is middling, and with chances this scarce at even strength, middling isn't enough to carry anything. The penalty kill is worse: 26th in the league, allowing 0.84 expected goals per game. Winnipeg takes 3.43 penalties a game and draws exactly the same number, so it isn't losing the discipline battle, but when it does go short-handed, opponents are getting good looks. Parity in penalties would be fine if the kill were average.

## The players driving it

Kyle Connor is the one clear bright spot. He has 11 goals and 15 points in 14 games, and his 7.51 individual expected goals lead the team, so he is getting the shots to justify the production. He has scored 3.48 more goals than expected, which suggests some of it will cool. The team is also 8.39 percentage points better in expected-goal share with him on the ice.

Mark Scheifele has 12 points but only 2 goals, 3.1 fewer than his chances would predict, and the team is 7.78 points better with him out there. Evolving-Hockey's wins above replacement, a single number for how many wins a player adds over a freely available replacement, has him at 3 for the 2025-26 season, tops on the roster. Gabriel Vilardi (1 goal, 3.3 below expected) and Dawson Mercer (0 goals, 2.63 below) are also finishing well under their chances, which helps explain the 6.6-goal team shortfall.

Cole Perfetti is the most interesting case. He has 6 goals and 11 points, and the team's expected-goal share is 11.94 points better with him on the ice, the biggest swing on the roster. He is playing 18:45 a night, up from 15:37, and is on the ice for 95% of the team's power-play chances, up from 50%. His own chances are up to 1.40 expected goals per 60 minutes from 1.08. Fourteen games is a small sample, but ice time settles faster than scoring does, and the usage looks real. Dylan Samberg (11.9 points better) is the other player who consistently tilts the ice.

The video titles around the team hint at the response. One listed on October 30 reads "Arniel Splits Up Connor & Scheifele," so the coaching staff has been reshuffling the top forwards.

## Will it hold?

Mostly, yes, with one caveat. A 45% expected-goal share is a bottom-five process, and the 27th-place points ranking is about where the chances say this team belongs. The luck is split: finishing has been 6.6 goals unkind, while goaltending has been kind. If the shooters regress upward, some of the scoring gap should close, and a few of the one-goal losses would flip. But the underlying problem is that Winnipeg concedes far more quality than it creates, and finishing luck can't fix that.

## What to watch

First, whether splitting Connor and Scheifele raises the team's share of chances or just spreads the same output across two lines. Second, the penalty kill, because a 26th-place unit is the easiest part of this team to improve. Third, the schedule, which Fink flagged: FLA, CAR, MTL, VAN, TBL and NJD are coming. Winnipeg already lost to MTL despite winning the chance battle, and a turn of finishing luck there would be the first sign the slide is easing. Until the chances improve, though, the standings are likely to keep reflecting how the Jets are playing.
